evidence_add.locator: eMethods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (begins p. 5; the model, covariate and interaction sentences on p. 6) (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/VickersSmith_2025_Supplement.pdf)
evidence_add.extracted: Each GEE model included baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, and, for each drug-use day, drug category, study week and part of the week; education, employment, ever having received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose entered the behaviour models only, and the daily composite score and the number of times strips were used entered the nonfatal overdose model only (the same sets as the article's Table 3 notes d and g; injecting is not a covariate in any model). Whether the association with the composite score and with nonfatal overdose was modified was tested by two-way interactions of baseline strip use with state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and study week, and, for overdose only, daily injection: seven modifiers for overdose and six for the composite score. A missing-at-random mixed model was fitted for the composite score only; all P values are called descriptive.

evidence_add.locator: eFigure 5 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/VickersSmith_2025_Supplement.pdf); publisher HTML: Results › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose, 1st paragraph
evidence_add.extracted: eFigure 5 plots, for each group, the adjusted mean daily probability of a self-reported nonfatal overdose across the 28-day observation period against age, on a log scale; the article's Results say the association was modified by age in adjusted but not in unadjusted analyses, and give no age-specific ratios. Editors' reading of the figure (measured from the image): the probabilities are drawn with 95% bands over ages 19 to 76; the strip group's line falls steeply with age while the comparison group's stays nearly flat, the two crossing at about age 42, so the modelled risk is higher in the strip group among younger and lower among older participants; the two bands overlap at every age; the plotted probabilities (about 0.0003 to 0.014 in the strip group and 0.002 to 0.003 in the comparison group) are well below the mean daily risk of 0.02 in the article's Table 3, so they were computed at covariate values the figure does not state.

change: Supplement reading, 27 October 2026: the age modification of the overdose estimate (P = .02) is now qualified from the supplement: in eFigure 5 the strip group's modelled risk is higher among younger and lower among older participants, but the 95% bands overlap at every age, and the eMethods show that age was one of seven modifiers tested for overdose (13 tests across the two outcomes), the only one reported; the article adds that age did not modify the association without adjustment (two new anchors, supplement pp. 5–6 and p. 22). The eMethods also confirm the covariates of the overdose model given in the Table 3 note g anchor, and eFigure 4 (raw daily shares higher in the strip group on 25 of 28 days) agrees with the unadjusted risk ratio of 2.06, so the statement is unchanged (AI reader 152, supplement reader). No rating or status flag changed; the new anchors are ai-located until another reader checks them at the stated place.

evidence_set: At baseline, people who used strips already had a higher composite score and number of overdose risk-reduction behaviours over the past 30 days (called means in the text; eTable 4 gives medians), and a higher prevalence of nearly every behaviour across most drug categories, except use by routes other than injection, which was more common among people who did not use strips (values in eTables 4 and 5 of the supplement; see the supplement anchor).

evidence_add.extracted: Overdose risk-reduction behaviours over the past 30 days at baseline, 414 people who had used strips against 312 who had not (the 726 in the analysed sample who used drugs in the past 30 days): composite score median 8.0 (quartiles 7.0–10.0) against 7.0 (5.0–8.0) and number of behaviours median 6.0 (5.0–7.0) against 5.0 (4.0–6.0), each P < .001 (both missing for 112); answering always: naloxone nearby 267 of 414 (64.5%) against 121 of 312 (38.8%), someone else present 53.4% against 43.3%, testing the strength of drugs 36.5% against 17.0% (never 14.7% against 53.8%), using slowly 33.1% against 19.9%, asking someone to check on them 27.3% against 9.3%, watching someone use the same drugs first 15.7% against 9.0%, and using by routes other than injection 32.4% against 41.5%. The table gives medians, not the means the article's text names. Editors' calculation: 267 of 414 is 64.49%, 64 in 100; 121 of 312 is 38.78%, 39 in 100.
